claims.text: The as-cast alloy initially consists of a homogeneous metastable solid solution with Mg uniformly distributed among the other elements.
The initial alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
Thermal aging promotes phase separation and evolution of the metastable structure toward a stable structure.
During thermal aging, Mg segregates into Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Thermal aging produces grain-boundary or phase refinement associated with Mg-rich precipitation.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates act as sites for preferential Mg segregation at the alloy surface.
Thermal energy enables Mg to partition out of a supersaturated BCC or FCC solid solution into stable intermetallic phases.
Mg partitioning changes the local chemical environment at grain boundaries and at the alloy surface.
The altered surface chemistry promotes formation of a thin, adherent, Mg-enriched oxide scale during high-temperature exposure.
The Mg-enriched oxide scale is thinner, more uniform, and more protective after aging than the oxide scale on the as-cast alloy.
The changed oxide composition improves high-temperature oxidation resistance and reduces oxidation spallation relative to the as-cast alloy.
Refined interphase boundaries and changed surface chemistry lower corrosion current density relative to the as-cast alloy.
Thermally aged material exhibits improved passivation behavior in corrosive media relative to the as-cast material.
The as-cast baseline contains no significant intermetallic phase formation.
The as-cast baseline has a higher corrosion rate and greater oxidation spallation than the aged alloy.
Differences in constituent elemental properties are sufficient to promote stable intermetallic formation under suitable thermal conditions.
Processing conditions that preclude phase evolution will not produce the proposed segregation-mediated corrosion and oxidation response.
